title: What's still to play for in the F1 driver market?
excerpt:
We've seen more driver market dominos fall in the last couple of weeks, with Max Verstappen confirming he's staying put at Red Bull not just for next season but until the end of 2030, while Alpine announced last week they've re-signed Franco Colapinto alongside Pierre Gasly. So what's still to play for and who holds the key?

Most teams are choosing stability rather than trying something new and thus we've seen a host of renewals rather than unveilings of new faces of late.

McLaren are sorted for next year with Lando Norris – who recently extended his deal by a few years to keep him at the team until at least the end of 2030 – alongside Oscar Piastri, while Ferrari are sticking with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

title: Five current drivers compared to past F1 stars

title: Aron set for next FP1 run with Alpine at Monza
excerpt:
Alpine have confirmed that reserve driver Paul Aron will participate in another Free Practice 1 outing for the squad at this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix.

Aron has previously been in action during three practice sessions so far in 2026, with the first in Barcelona and Austria being with Audi as part of an agreement between the two teams.

The Estonian went on to drive for Alpine in Hungary and will again get behind the wheel of the A526 when Friday’s track running kicks off in Monza, sitting in for Pierre Gasly.

From there Aron will embark on a busy weekend, as he will head back to the team’s Enstone base for simulator work in the evening after his FP1 run in order to help with fine-tuning the car’s set-up.

“I am looking forward to driving again in Free Practice 1 with the team this weekend,” said Aron. “I am grateful to the team for giving me the opportunity to get back behind the wheel so soon.

“I was very pleased with my session in Budapest, and I hope to build on it this time around, particularly helping the team compare our latest upgrade package which I have driven in the simulator.

“It's going to be a busy weekend for me as I'll be on the simulator at Enstone on Friday night to further help the team fine tune the set-up before returning to the track on Saturday. I'll give it my all to hopefully assist the team in having a successful weekend.”

The weekend at Monza will also see both Gasly and Franco Colapinto run the upgrade package that was first introduced on Gasly’s car last time out in Zandvoort.

title: What do McLaren’s newest upgrades tell us ahead of Monza?
excerpt:
On top of Hungary’s all-new floor, wakeboards and floor slots, McLaren brought to Zandvoort a new rear wing, engine cover, diffuser tweaks and new front wheel rims as further discrete performance items.

“The items aren’t linked as a package,” explained McLaren’s technical director Neil Houldey of the Zandvoort parts. “They all provide aero performance as individual components and don’t need each other to perform.”

This double hit of upgrades in consecutive races proved very powerful and helped Lando Norris to back-to-back Grand Prix victories, both of them from pole position.

title: Ferrari reveal special Schumacher-inspired livery for Monza
excerpt:
Ferrari have presented a special one-off livery for their home race at Monza, paying tribute to seven-time World Champion Michael Schumacher.

It is now 30 years since the German joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final victory with the team – scored at the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

As well as claiming five of his world titles with the Maranello-based squad, Schumacher bagged five Monza wins in red (in 1996, 1998, 2000, 2003 and 2006).

Heading into the weekend, Ferrari revealed bespoke race suits that will be worn by current drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, featuring Schumacher’s logo and the seven stars he used to carry on his helmet to signify his seven titles.

On Tuesday morning, the outfit followed up on those comments by showcasing a Schumacher-inspired car livery, again noting the details above around their usual 2026 design.

Ferrari explained that this week’s wide-ranging tributes are inspired by Schumacher’s “impact on the racing world” and “his enduring mindset”.

title: 7 memorable Italian Grand Prix moments from Monza
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix is only a few days away, and Monza is ready to welcome the teams, drivers and fans in typical Italian fashion. From teary moments to the Tifosi showing up in style, the fastest circuit in Formula 1 has never lacked entertainment on or off the track.

Monza was on the F1 calendar from the very beginning and has hosted all Italian Grands Prix but one since 1950. Here are some of the most unforgettable moments from the Temple of Speed in recent racing history...

Leclerc delights the Tifosi

There's arguably nothing more special for an F1 driver than winning for Ferrari on home soil at Monza – something Charles Leclerc acheived in 2019 when he topped the podium in Italy, taking his second career win in Formula 1 and his first at Monza.

“There were people as far as I could see,” he said afterwards. “It was packed. I was trying to find my mum. She was in a grandstand... I was trying to find her but there were way too many people.”

Schumacher equals Senna's tally

No driver has won more races for Ferrari than the great Michael Schumacher, but perhaps one of his most emotional victories was in the 2000 Italian Grand Prix?

After missing the previous year’s Grand Prix, the German driver returned to Monza in top shape, winning the race in front of the Tifosi. It was his 41st career victory, meaning he equalled the tally Ayrton Senna – something a very emotional Schumacher was reminded about in the post-race press conference.

Ferrari turns 90

Ferrari chose the weekend of the Italian Grand Prix to celebrate their 90th anniversary in 2019, when they took over Piazza Duomo in Milan to hold a special “90 years of emotions” event which saw Charles Leclerc and Sebastian Vettel alongside drivers and management from the past, marking the storied history of the Maranello team in front of a sea of red jerseys and caps with the iconic Duomo di Milano as a backdrop.

The Tifosi gather at the Piazza Duomo during the “90 Years of Emotion” event in 2019

A host of former Ferrari drivers were in attendance

Piazza Duomo was the setting for Ferrari's 90th year celebration

A maiden victory for Gasly

Monza without grandstands packed with passionate supporters is almost impossible to imagine. But in 2020 – due to the Covid pandemic – the Italian Grand Prix was held behind closed doors, and in an empty venue, Pierre Gasly found his way to success.

The French driver, wearing the colours of the other Italian team – then known as AlphaTauri – raced to his first ever Formula 1 victory.

Vettel's first triumph

But Gasly's win in 2020 wasn't the first time a driver from 'Italy's other team' had raced to a maiden victory at Monza.

Sebastian Vettel was in just his first full season as an F1 driver when he claimed a shock pole position for Toro Rosso at the Italian Grand Prix – and then followed that up with his first ever win.

The shoey returns

The Italian Grand Prix holds a special place in Daniel Ricciardo’s heart. The Australian won at Monza for McLaren in 2021, three years after his last victory. But it wasn’t a lucky win – Ricciardo led the race from start to finish and after a 1,204-day wait, he was back on the top of the podium ahead of his team mate Lando Norris, and Valtteri Bottas.

And what a better way to celebrate the long-awaited win with the iconic shoey celebration including Norris and McLaren boss Zak Brown?

Hamilton arriving in Monza in style

More recently, Sir Lewis Hamilton wanted to show up in style for his first Italian Grand Prix as a Ferrari driver – and he did not disappoint.

The seven-time world champion arrived at the circuit for last year's event riding a motorbike in the colours of the Italian flag.

He went on to finish sixth in that race, but will be hoping he can challenge for victory this weekend, after he took his first Grand Prix win in red earlier this year in Barcelona.

title: 5 storylines we’re excited about ahead of the Italian GP
excerpt:
The second half of the season is well and truly underway and the final two European rounds take place over a double-header that kicks off in Italy. With McLaren resurgent but plenty for the home fans to get excited about, there are sure to be a number of talking points when the paddock arrives in Monza.

Antonelli set for a home race penalty

Given the support Ferrari always receive at Monza, the Italian fans could find themselves slightly torn this weekend, as Kimi Antonelli arrives at his home race as the championship leader.

Rewind 12 months and it would have been a surprising prediction to suggest Antonelli would be 59 points clear in the standings in just his second season in Formula 1, even with the expectation that Mercedes would deliver a championship-contending car.

Yet as the Silver Arrows continue to prioritise the best approach to the season as a whole – rather than any individual race – Antonelli will face a tall order to secure victory in his home Grand Prix due to a planned power unit penalty.

Reliability issues mean Mercedes believe they won’t make it to the end of the season without taking a penalty with each car at some stage, and they also have the potential to upgrade the power unit through the FIA’s Advanced Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) mechanism.

Whether it is a new specification that is introduced at Monza or not, the team have confirmed Antonelli will take a full new power unit and start towards the back of the grid.

“With Kimi, we're taking the full thing,” Toto Wolff said in Zandvoort. “Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it. Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR.”

Wolff confirms Antonelli is set for grid penalty at Monza

Red Bull’s driver situation

The summer shutdown ended with an unexpected driver line-up change – albeit only a temporary one – at Red Bull, after Isack Hadjar injured his wrist ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix, ruling him out of the race weekend at Zandvoort.

Liam Lawson was promoted in his place, and impressed despite the lack of practice mileage on offer during the Sprint weekend. By Saturday’s Qualifying session, Lawson was able to get close to Max Verstappen and secured a spot alongside his team mate on the fourth row, before a solid run to seventh place behind the McLaren, Mercedes and Ferrari cars.

With Lawson at Red Bull, Yuki Tsunoda returned at Racing Bulls and also had a strong weekend, just missing out on points. So both proved to be strong replacements while Hadjar recovers.

It has not yet been confirmed if Hadjar will be fit to return this weekend at Monza, but if not then it is expected that Red Bull will stick with the Zandvoort line-ups, giving both Lawson and Tsunoda another chance to impress. While it will be a race on a very different type of circuit, they would have three practice sessions to help them build on top of their previous weekend’s experience.

Stability in the driver market

In the build-up to the Dutch Grand Prix weekend, three driver contracts were confirmed that suggested there will be little movement across the grid in 2027.

First up was Alex Albon remaining with Williams, shortly followed by his team mate Carlos Sainz also committing his future to the team and ensuring an unchanged driver line-up for James Vowles to work with next year.

Then came the big news of Max Verstappen extending his Red Bull stay until at least the end of 2030, as the Dutchman reaffirmed his intention to complete his whole career with the team.

Since leaving the Netherlands, there has been further confirmation of a driver retaining their seat, as Franco Colapinto’s strong season has been rewarded with another year at Alpine alongside Pierre Gasly.

As it stands, there have only been extensions and renewals confirmed – with Lando Norris and McLaren also committing long-term to each other – as the driver market has stabilised this year. Aston Martin are a team of interest as Fernando Alonso has yet to announce his plans for 2027, while there could potentially be movement at Haas and Racing Bulls.

Ollie Bearman is expected to continue with Haas, and Esteban Ocon’s recent form shows he is doing everything he can to remain alongside him, but both seats are currently still available.

Although unconfirmed at this stage, it would be a major surprise if Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad don’t keep their seats at Red Bull and Racing Bulls respectively, while Lawson’s substitute appearance keeps him in the mix for another season despite the emergence of Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov.

Why Norris and McLaren have committed to each other for the long term

The Tifosi

Sure, Kimi Antonelli is leading the Drivers’ Championship, but you can still expect to see a sea of red at Monza as the Tifosi come out in force.

Although McLaren have won the past two races, Ferrari have been Mercedes’ closest challenger on average this season, with Lewis Hamilton sitting joint-second in the standings, 59 points adrift of Antonelli.

The expected penalty for Antonelli should only serve to increase Ferrari’s chances of fighting for victory at their home race, as they look to make inroads into Mercedes’ 87-point lead in the Constructors’ Championship.

Racing at Monza in front of such a passionate fanbase is always a sight to behold during the year, and if one of Hamilton or Charles Leclerc can deliver a win then the atmosphere underneath the iconic podium will be something particularly special.

Celebrating a legend

Aside from Ferrari’s own hopes of victory, they will be paying tribute to one of the most successful drivers in Formula 1 history this coming weekend.

Michael Schumacher won five of his seven drivers’ titles with Ferrari from 2000-2004, but 2026 marks 30 years since the legendary German joined the team, and 20 years since his final Monza victory for the Scuderia – on the same weekend he announced his first retirement from the sport.

It took five years to taste championship success, but there were still three race wins in his first season in red back in 1996 – including at Monza – as Schumacher secured a victory in each of his 11 seasons with Ferrari.

The team have revealed special race suits that will be worn by Hamilton and Leclerc that feature Schumacher’s logo and the seven stars he used to carry on his helmet design to signify his seven world titles. Ferrari say this week’s tributes are inspired by Schumacher’s “impact on the racing world” and “his enduring mindset”.

title: Vowles admits he worried about losing both Sainz and Albon
excerpt:
James Vowles has admitted that he was concerned by the possibility of Williams losing both Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon amid the team’s struggles this season, and says the confirmation both drivers will be staying on for next year has seen a “weight lifted” off the factory.

The 2025 campaign saw the Grove-based outfit climb from their previous ninth in the championship to an impressive fifth, a run of form that included two podium finishes for Sainz.

Things have proven much more challenging for Williams in 2026, however, with the team back down to P9 after only scoring 11 points so far. Despite the difficulties, both Sainz and Albon were recently confirmed as staying with the squad into next season.

Speaking to the media during the Dutch Grand Prix weekend – days on from the announcements – Vowles was asked whether he had been worried about losing them.

“[I was] concerned about losing both, because they are World Championship-material drivers that deserve the opportunity to be fighting for podiums or more, and we haven't delivered that,” he explained.

“And more than that, we had a scope of where we were moving to. I think that there's no doubt if you sort of look to the outside – I hope there's no doubt – over the last few years, we've been slowly stepping forward with last year being a blip. I think [it was] too positive from where we were, but a step in the right direction.

“So for us to move backwards isn't just a surprise to the drivers, it's a surprise to everyone else, and that will always create risk that you lose them. What I'm thankful for is, the moment we had problems, they stood by our side.

“There wasn't finger pointing, it was actually, ‘tell me what I can do’, and they both came into the factory, spoke to the whole organisation and gave them a lift. Carlos did the same and Alex did the same this week once they re-signed.

“They wanted to make sure that they were here with the team. They want this to be a part of them, that is here on a turnaround of this organisation, and I'm thankful for that. But it's also an indication of what we've shown them in the back end of what's happened and what we're doing about it.”

Albon and Sainz explain why they have kept faith in Williams

Vowles went on to outline why retaining Sainz and Albon was “incredibly important” to him.

“[Reason number] one, it shows the outside world – I can't tell you everything that's going on behind the scenes, but I can tell them, and if they are re-signing it will give you an indication that there's a lot of change ongoing and they believe in what the future looks like.

“And that belief is incredibly important, whether it's for team members or for anyone in the outside world.

“Number two, that consistency is important because the team is really maturing and changing and, as much as you can keep consistent, especially in a driver line-up, it becomes desperately important in order to keep building on that.

“Probably the best way to summarise it to you is [that in] the factory, there's a weight lifted off it this week as the result of it and I've seen them move forward at a much faster pace as a result, so the belief is real and tangible.”

With Albon’s re-signing publicly confirmed first before Sainz’s followed one day later, Vowles also suggested that there was a reason behind the separate announcements.

“For me, and for the drivers, it was important to state that they are different stories and different timings,” the Team Principal said.

“Also, it helped me because Alex was in the simulator on Tuesday and Carlos on Wednesday. I was able to show them to the team and I didn't have them both on the same day at the same time!

“But for me, they're different journeys. Alex has been here since 2022. He has dedicated so much of his life to this project and he wants it to be successful, and I think that's one message in its own right.

“With Carlos, what he needed was to be demonstrated what's happening behind the scenes and he wanted to then commit into the long term, and it's a very different set of arrangements that we have between the two of them. I think the messaging is no different though.

“We all have unfinished business. Our goal is to have Alex and Carlos by our side for many years to come. We have to do work on our side in order to make sure we are stepping up, irrespective of our drivers. The drivers are not the limitation to us at the moment. We are.

“We have to fix that, and quickly, for us more than anything else. But the announcements of the drivers will show you that there's belief in the project for the long term, and that individuals, even the ones that have been here since ‘22, can see the change and want to be a part of it.”

title: Liam Lawson handed 'mentally tougher' verdict after Red Bull axe
excerpt:
Former Haas F1 team principal Guenther Steiner believes Liam Lawson is “mentally tougher” as a result of his demotion from Red Bull last year.

Lawson lasted just two rounds at the Milton Keynes-based squad last year as he struggled for form alongside Max Verstappen.

However, he got a second chance last time out at the Dutch Grand Prix as he was called up to replace an injured Isack Hadjar.

The New Zealander impressed as he lapped close to Verstappen before ending the race in seventh place, adding more points to his tally.

Steiner detailed the performance showcased how much more confidence he now possesses compared to 18 months ago.

“Last year's car was difficult to drive for anybody,” Steiner told the Red Flags podcast.

“I would also say Liam was not given enough time, as well. He has another year under his belt.

“What he went through there made him tougher mentally, because that's not easy to [endure].

“And now he goes in a Red Bull and has got quite a good level of confidence.”

One major difference at Red Bull this year is the absence of Helmut Marko, who was often very strict when it came to driver line-ups.

Steiner believes Marko's exit at the end of 2025 has put less pressure on Lawson's shoulders.

“He doesn't need to look over his shoulder all the time because one guy is not there anymore as well, which always was asking immediately if somebody wasn't bringing the performance,” he said.

“It was just also yet more experience, a different car. I think they are a little bit easier to drive than the cars from last year, the ground effect cars.

“Mentally, he was like 'I cannot lose here. I do the best with what I can. I don't focus on Max. I do my thing and try to do the best'.

“A lot of little things coming together, and all of a sudden it worked.”

title: Red Bull announce signing of senior Aston Martin figure to replace Gianpiero Lambiase
excerpt:
Red Bull has announced the signing of Tom McCullough from Aston Martin as its future head of racing.

He will join the Milton Keynes-based team in early 2027, after serving a period of gardenning leave from the Aston Martin group, and be the de facto replacement for the outgoing Gianpiero Lambiase, who will leave the team next year.

McCullough, who has enjoyed spells with Reynard Engineering, Williams, and Sauber, joined Aston Martin when it was Force India in 2014, originally as chief race engineer, before climbing to performance director in January 2018.

However, in January 2025, he was re-assigned from the F1 team after poor performances across the second-half of 2023 and through 2024, across to the performance directorship of Aston Martin Performance Technologies.

He was announced as leaving the Aston Martin group entirely in August 2026, and has now joined Red Bull in the newly-created role of 'head of racing.'

"We're delighted to welcome Tom to the team at the beginning of 2027, and look forward to the wealth of experience and expertise he will bring to the role," read a short Red Bull statement.

His signing is the second big-name Red Bull has lured from another team, after the capture of Gwen Lagrue from Mercedes as young driver advisor.

McCullough's signing comes as the team prepares for life after Lambiase, with the head of race engineering, and Max Verstappen's engineer, agreeing to join McLaren, with this expected to be from the 2028 season.

Other senior figures, such as chief designer Craig Skinner have also left, with a reshuffle seeing Ben Waterhouse becoming chief performance and design engineer, with Andrea Landi joining from Racing Bulls as head of performance.

title: Car flip and F1's closest ever finish: Five dramatic moments from the Italian GP
excerpt:
The Italian Grand Prix takes place this weekend, and it has served up its fair share of dramatic moments throughout its history.

Monza has a unique ability to deliver chaos, heartbreak and euphoria in equal measure. Few circuits on the calendar can match the sheer emotional range of the Italian Grand Prix, a race that has, time and again, produced moments that define entire eras of the sport.

As Ferrari's Charles Leclerc put it ahead of the 2025 edition of the race: "Monza is Monza, and I'll never stop trying. Winning on this track, in front of our tifosi, is so special that I can only have one goal this weekend."

But that emotional pull extends well beyond the Scuderia.

Here are five moments that encapsulate why the Italian Grand Prix remains one of the most dramatic fixtures on the F1 calendar.

The closest finish in F1 history, 1971

Before chicanes were installed to tame Monza's fearsome speeds, the old circuit was a slipstreaming playground.

The 1971 Italian Grand Prix remains the ultimate example. Peter Gethin, who started 11th, fought his way through a pack of cars that swapped positions relentlessly across 55 laps, with around 25 lead changes involving eight different drivers.

On the final lap, Gethin over-revved his BRM V12 engine out of Parabolica and edged ahead to beat Ronnie Peterson by just 0.01 seconds.

The top five were separated by a mere 0.61 seconds. It was Gethin's only F1 victory, and it remains the closest finish the sport has ever seen.

Senna's backmarker heartbreak denies McLaren a perfect season, 1988

McLaren had won every single race of the 1988 season heading into Monza, and Ayrton Senna looked set to continue that dominance and complete an unprecedented clean sweep.

With just two laps remaining, Senna led comfortably when he moved to lap Jean-Louis Schlesser's Williams at the Rettifilo chicane. Schlesser, substituting for the unwell Nigel Mansell, cut back unexpectedly and made contact with the McLaren's right rear, breaking its suspension and beaching Senna on a kerb.

Gerhard Berger and Michele Alboreto swept through in their Ferraris to complete a stunning 1-2, less than a month after Enzo Ferrari's death on 14 August.

McLaren finished the season with 15 wins from 16 races, an all-time record for dominance, but Monza ensured that a perfect, 16-from-16 season would remain forever out of reach.

Fittipaldi's last-lap backflip stuns Monza, 1993

The 1993 Italian Grand Prix produced one of the most astonishing moments ever witnessed at a finish line.

Running in eighth place on the final lap, Christian Fittipaldi attempted to overtake his own Minardi teammate Pierluigi Martini for seventh position down the main straight at close to 300 km/h.

As he pulled alongside, his left-front wheel clipped Martini's right-rear, and the impact acted as a ramp, launching Fittipaldi's car into the air and sending it through a full backward somersault.

The Minardi landed back on all four wheels, still pointing in the right direction, and skidded across the finish line. Fittipaldi was classified eighth. Neither driver was injured, and the moment remains one of the most spectacular in the sport's history.

Hamilton's pit lane blunder gifts Gasly a fairy tale, 2020

Lewis Hamilton was cruising to a comfortable victory at the 2020 Italian Grand Prix when Kevin Magnussen's retirement brought out the Safety Car.

Race control closed the pit lane, but Hamilton pitted regardless, the result of a communication breakdown with his Mercedes team. The resulting 10-second stop-and-go penalty dropped him to last.

A red flag for Charles Leclerc's heavy crash at Parabolica further reshuffled the order, and when the dust settled, Pierre Gasly found himself leading for AlphaTauri.

He held off Carlos Sainz by just 0.415 seconds to take a remarkable maiden victory, the team's first win since Sebastian Vettel triumphed at the same circuit in 2008.

Verstappen lands on Hamilton, 2021

The 2021 championship battle between Max Verstappen and Hamilton reached boiling point at Monza. After slow pit stops dropped both into each other's path, they arrived side by side at the Turn 1-2 chicane on lap 26.

Verstappen, attempting to pass around the outside, was squeezed towards the inside kerb at Turn 2, where his Red Bull struck the notorious sausage kerb and was launched into the air, landing directly on top of Hamilton's Mercedes.

The halo device was widely credited with preventing serious injury. Both retired on the spot, and stewards later judged Verstappen predominantly at fault, handing him a three-place grid penalty for the following race.

Daniel Ricciardo, meanwhile, led Lando Norris home for a McLaren 1-2, their first victory since 2012.

title: Honda outline Italian GP priority ahead of 'realistic' test
excerpt:
Honda has outlined its primary focus for the Italian Grand Prix this weekend as it gets its upgraded power unit back on track at Monza.

The Japanese manufacturer finally unveiled its new engine last time out at Zandvoort as it continues to make progress following its difficult start to the new season.

Its upgraded power unit came shortly after Aston Martin introduced a substantially modified package of its own.

Having lifted itself off the bottom of the standings, Aston Martin-Honda is seeking to get involved in regular contention for the point-scoring results.

However, with Monza being heavily reliant on strong straight-line speed, Honda insisted it must be “realistic” about the weekend ahead.

“Monza is a unique circuit with one of the highest full-throttle ratios on the 2026 calendar, with its long straights and only 11 corners,” said Honda's chief F1 engineer Shintaro Orihara.

“At this track, how you distribute the limited energy across these sections becomes crucial, and this is especially amplified in qualifying.

“The lap times at Monza are highly sensitive to power. With the introduction of our spec 2 engine in Zandvoort, we have made a step forward in terms of performance, but we need to be realistic about the upcoming weekend as we know that we are still behind our competitors in terms of overall power.”

Aston Martin managed to get itself into the points last time out in the Netherlands, with Fernando Alonso crossing the line in ninth place.

However, Honda has suggested it will not be focusing primarily on the results at Monza as it looks to improve the drivability of its engine.

“Our key focus at the Italian Grand Prix is to improve driveability,” Orihara said.

“Since the Dutch Grand Prix, we have been working a lot on the dyno at HRC Sakura to improve this and, specifically, to achieve stable and consistent combustion control.

“At Monza, we will be confirming the effect of that work and carrying out further tuning, which will give us more competitiveness in the coming races.”

title: Colton Herta handed latest F1 opportunity by Cadillac
excerpt:
Colton Herta will take part in the opening practice session this weekend at Monza for Cadillac, the team has confirmed.

Herta joined the American squad as a test and development driver for the 2026 campaign, which came with the guarantee of several FP1 outings.

Having stepped into the cockpit already in Barcelona and Hungary, Herta will have his third outing of the year this weekend at the Italian Grand Prix.

The 26-year-old will take over driving duties from Sergio Perez before the latter returns to the seat for FP2.

“This is an excellent opportunity to experience different aspects of the MAC-26,” Herta said.

“Having driven on the high-downforce tracks in Barcelona and Budapest, the challenge will be very different in Monza.

“With the car set up for low drag, it will move around more, placing a greater emphasis on accuracy at the braking points and on threading the eye of a needle across the curbs in the chicanes.

“I’m really excited to be able to contribute to the race weekend and to the team’s further development at one of the most iconic circuits in motorsport.”

Herta is vying for a full-time seat with Cadillac in 2027, and his F1 outing will coincide with his F2 programme that continues this weekend at Monza.

title: McLaren confirm return of eye-catching F1 upgrade at Italian GP
excerpt:
McLaren has confirmed it will race its rotating 'Macarena' rear wing at the Italian Grand Prix, giving the concept its first competitive outing on the MCL40.

The team calls its version the H-Wing, a nod to the 'H' in Etihad Airways branding on the rear wing.

The team has detailed it mirrors the logic behind McLaren's 2010 F-duct name, which came from the Vodafone 'F' placed near the MP4-25's air inlet.

The concept first ran in practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix, when reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli evaluated it on Oscar Piastri's car in FP1.

That test focused on controlled aero runs and braking checks before the wing was removed ahead of qualifying. Andrea Stella described it as a "positive sign-off" and said McLaren was preparing to introduce it at future events.

It has now been confirmed it will be in use at Monza this weekend as McLaren continues to its momentum, having won two races on the bounce.

The Macarena wing was first spotted at pre-season testing by Ferrari and has since been adopted by Red Bull - albeit the design has been sidelined following a series of high-speed spins for Max Verstappen.

“This weekend, we have brought what we believe is needed to be competitive, including a new low-drag rear wing specification, including the first use of our H-Wing, alongside some small aerodynamic and low-drag options that we will evaluate before deciding the final specification for Qualifying,” technical director Neil Houdley said.

“Overall, we know there is still more performance to unlock from the MCL40, both through maximising the package we already have and through further upgrades planned for the races ahead.”

title: George Russell handed Italian GP ultimatum: 'It's now or never'
excerpt:
Former F1 driver Jolyon Palmer has stated it is critical for George Russell to win the Italian Grand Prix for his title hopes this year.

Russell currently sits 59 points behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli in the drivers' championship, with the Italian enjoying the lion's share of Mercedes' success so far in 2026.

However, Antonelli has already confirmed that he will take a grid penalty this weekend at Monza, despite it being his home race.

The 19-year-old will be fitted with a brand new power unit for the event as Mercedes, offering Russell a chance to gain points, should he finish ahead.

With the second half of the campaign now in full swing, Palmer highlighted the importance of the event for Russell.

“Reliability is not going to be easy at Monza,” Palmer told the F1 Nation podcast.

“If Kimi wins in Monza with a grid penalty, he is champion - I'll go as far as saying that.

“It'll be such a crushing blow. He will have won his home race with a load of overtaking, huge aplomb and it will suck the life out of George to not take points out of him in Monza.

“George has to win this.”

Despite losing further ground to Antonelli last time out at Zandvoort, Palmer insisted Russell can take encouragement from his own performance.

“He knows Kimi has a grid drop. He knows that he's got a golden shot to back up what was a solid weekend in Zandvoort,” he said.

“He outqualified Kimi, he took sprint pole, won the sprint. If he didn't get such bad starts in the race, possibly he could actually have beaten Kimi in the race.

“I don't think the pace difference was enough for Kimi just to blast past him.

“So I think George will be thinking, 'Again, it's now or never'.”

title: FIA president voices support for F1 return to 'historic' country
excerpt:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has voiced his support for the return of a grand prix event to Argentina.

The country last featured on the Formula 1 calendar in 1998 and has been absent for nearly three decades, but fresh momentum behind a potential return continues to build.

Argentina's history in Formula 1 stretches back to the very early days of the championship, with the first Argentine Grand Prix held in Buenos Aires in 1953 being the first world championship event to take place outside of Europe.

The country now has a fresh connection through Franco Colapinto, who races for Alpine and has just been confirmed on the 2027 grid alongside Pierre Gasly.

Offering his backing, Ben Sulayem told A24: "I will support the initiative to have an F1 race or the World Rally Championship here in Argentina.

"We need to develop venues for sustainable races, where there is the willingness, the investments, the fans, and the government's power to make it happen.

"Does Argentina deserve to be part of the F1 calendar? The answer is yes. They have history, they have a track record; the first race was held here in 1953."

Argentina is far from the only country pushing for a place on the calendar. Thailand has advanced furthest, with its cabinet approving a proposal for a Bangkok street race reportedly targeting 2028.

South Africa, Rwanda, South Korea and Turkey have also expressed interest.

With the calendar already running at 24 races in recent seasons and demand from across the globe continuing to grow, finding space for new venues remains one of F1's biggest challenges.

title: Alpine announce Pierre Gasly replacement for first Italian Grand Prix practice
excerpt:
Paul Aron is to deputise for Pierre Gasly at Alpine in this weekend's opening practice session for the Italian Grand Prix.

It is the first session of the year Gasly will have missed as the Estonian takes over driving the A526 machine, having done so for Franco Colapinto at the Hungarian Grand Prix.

Both Gasly and Colapinto must miss one more FP1 session apiece in the remainder of the season to fulfill the regulations.

Aron has also taken part in two FP1 sessions for Audi in 2026, taking over from Nico Hulkenberg in Barcelona, and Gabriel Bortoleto in Austria.

The outing at Monza will be his ninth FP1 session in total since 2024, all coming for Stake/Audi and Alpine.

Aron is the second young driver confirmed for FP1, with Luke Browning once again driving for Williams.

"I am looking forward to driving again in Free Practice 1 with the team this weekend," said Aron.

"I am grateful to the team for giving me the opportunity to get back behind the wheel so soon. I was very pleased with my session in Budapest, and I hope to build on it this time around, particularly helping the team compare our latest upgrade package, which I have driven in the simulator.

"It's going to be a busy weekend for me as I'll be on the simulator at Enstone on Friday night to further help the team fine-tune the set-up before returning to the track on Saturday.

"I'll give it my all to hopefully assist the team in having a successful weekend."

title: Max Verstappen rumoured to make Mercedes GT3 return, 'seeking high-profile name for team-mate'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen may be set to make another appearance in the Verstappen Racing Mercedes-AMG GT3 this October.

A persistent rumour in the GT world suggests the Dutch driver will be on the starting grid in Portimão from October 16 through 18 during the final round of the GT World Challenge.

Should it happen, Verstappen is set to share the Mercedes-AMG GT3 with Chris Lulham, but the driver for the third seat has not yet been announced.

Daniel Juncadella and Jules Gounon, who are part of the regular lineup for this season’s endurance races, are seemingly unavailable due to their commitments in the World Endurance Championship.

This creates an opening for an interesting replacement alongside Verstappen and Lulham. Reportedly, the team is considering several options, with one notable name making the rounds: Alex Palou.

The IndyCar superstar is said to be a candidate to join the team in Portugal and is available, as the IndyCar season will be long over by then.

Verstappen himself is said to have expressed a preference for Palou as the third driver. Whether that wish will actually be granted remains unclear for now.

A return to the Mercedes-AMG GT3 would once again underscore just how seriously Verstappen takes his GT3 project, but his participation would mean he is in for some intense weeks.

The weekend before, he’ll race in the Singapore F1 Grand Prix; the weekend after, he’ll travel for the United States Grand Prix.

The Dutchman has recently become increasingly involved in the program and is combining his F1 career with appearances in endurance racing. Earlier this year, he already formed a successful partnership with Juncadella and Gounon.

A Mercedes spokesperson told RacingNews365: “On behalf of Mercedes-AMG Motorsport, I can neither confirm that Max Verstappen will take part in the final GT World Challenge round in Portimão, nor that Jules Gounon and Daniel Juncadella will miss the event.

“We are currently assessing various scenarios to ensure that we can compete effectively in Portimão with our teams.“

title: 2026 F1 Italian Grand Prix - Monza weather forecast
excerpt:
F1 drivers are set for an extremely hot weekend at the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, with the temperature expected to be in the mid-30 degree region.

Ahead of the trip to northern Italy, the current weather forecasts predict a rain-free weekend with sweltering conditions throughout, with Saturday's qualifying day currently expected to be the hottest of the three days of track action, topping the Mercury at 34 degrees Celsius.

Both Friday and Sunday are expected to max out at 33 degrees.

In terms of wind direction, drivers are set for a mixed bag, with changeable directions from session to session.

A headwind into big braking zones is ideal for drivers as it allows them to brake late, with the pit straight at Monza running directly north-south and the run through Curva Grande into the Variante della Roggia leaving drivers facing due east.

On Friday, the wind will be blowing from the east, southeast, before switching to from the south in the afternoon - a direct tailwind down the main straight.

For Saturday's qualifying, the winds will consistently come from the west, roughly corresponding to a headwind into the Ascari chicane but a tailwind into the della Roggia chicane.

For the race on Sunday, the winds will be coming from the east, corresponding to that precious headwind into the della Roggia, usually the best overtaking spot on the track aside from the Rettifilo chicane of Turns 1 and 2.

title: Toto Wolff 'under no illusion' at scale of renewed threat to Mercedes
excerpt:
Toto Wolff says Mercedes is "under no illusion" about how difficult the coming races will be for the team as F1 rivals close in on the championship leaders.

Mercedes started the campaign with the dominant car, and has won eight of the 12 races thus far, with Kimi Antonelli holding a 59-point advantage over team-mate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in the drivers' standings, and the team an 87-point buffer over Ferrari.

However, Mercedes has not brought any sizeable upgrades since May's Canadian GP, with Wolff saying after a Dutch GP where Antonelli claimed race-winner Lando Norris's McLaren was now "the car to beat" that the team was working in the "financial realities" of the cost cap and could not afford to bring as many regular upgrades as McLaren and Ferrari.

Furthermore, as the upgrade cycle continues, Antonelli is poised to take a dent in his points lead by taking a back-of-the-grid starting penalty for his home race by taking a full new power unit, which will be of the same specification as the existing units.

Looking ahead to the weekend, at a track Mercedes has not won at since Hamilton's 2018 win, Wolff feels that "the price of a mistake is much higher" as Mercedes' advantage is eroded.

"Monza and Madrid begin an important period for us. The field has compressed to the point where several teams can win on merit, and the price of a mistake is much higher," said Wolff.

"We have put ourselves in a strong position in both championships, but nobody in our team is under any illusion about how difficult the next races will be.

"For us, Monza begins with a challenge. Kimi will take a power unit penalty and start from the back of the grid. It's disappointing for him and for the fans who want to see him fighting from the front in his home race, but our sport doesn't reward sentiment.

"When you make decisions that benefit the championship campaign, sometimes you pay a short-term price. The objective now is straightforward: recover as many places as possible and maximise the points.

"On the other side of the garage, George arrives with good momentum after Zandvoort and will be looking to put himself firmly in the fight from the start of the weekend.

"Monza is an energy-poor track; you spend much of the lap asking everything from the power unit and don't have many opportunities to charge the battery.

"With the current regulations, that creates compromises that will need to be managed carefully. It is an interesting challenge and one that will likely lead to an exciting weekend."

title: Kimi Antonelli remains optimistic at Italian GP chances despite 'full thing' penalty
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli remains optimistic of his chances of success in the Italian Grand Prix, despite being set to take a huge grid penalty at his home race.

Antonelli will incur a back-of-the-grid drop at Monza after qualifying, after taking a complete new power unit of the same specification into his pool of parts.

The Italian has already used the maximum four Internal Combustion Engines (ICEs), and three energy stores and control electronics, in addition to four exhausts. He is still within tolerance of the turbocharger and MGU-K, but the decision has been taken to introduce a fully new unit for the title run-in.

Reflecting on that, in front of his home crowd, which means he can win qualifying but will not be starting on pole, Antonelli, who leads the drivers' standings by 59 points from team-mate George Russell and Lewis Hamilton in a points tie for second, was fully on board with the decision.

"Obviously, going into Monza [with the] engine penalty, I still think it’s the best track where to take it to," Antonelli told media, including RacingNews365.

"Of course, it’s my home race and all that kind of stuff, but I think it’s the best race to do so.

"So, I think it still will give me a chance to get a great result and bring home good points."

His boss Toto Wolff had previously spoken how the team's computer simulations had indicated Monza was the "best track" to take the required penalty.

"Our theory, our calculations say that it's the best track to take it," Wolff had said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't consider nationality when we have to fight for a championship and want to get the most PR, so that's what we're going to do."

Drivers are permitted a pool of components for the season, with the Italian driver having used four internal combustion engines, four exhausts, three energy stores (battery) and three control electronics – meaning he’s hit the permitted limits for these components. He still has one allowance for the turbocharger and MGU-K.

title: Sebastian Vettel to make special Ferrari return at Italian GP
excerpt:
Sebastian Vettel will get behind the wheel of a Ferrari car once again at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend, the team has confirmed.

Vettel raced for the Italian squad for six years, winning 14 grands prix for the team - the most behind Michael Schumacher and Niki Lauda.

Schumacher is being honoured by Ferrari at the Italian Grand Prix this weekend with the team introducing a throwback livery as it celebrates the seven-time champion's highly successful 10-year stint.

However, he his being celebrated even further as Vettel, along with Rubens Barrichello, will drive a lap around the track.

Barrichello, a long-time Ferrari team-mate of Schumacher, will get behind the wheel of the F2002 on Saturday around Monza.

Vettel, who has long shared a strong friendship with Schumacher, will have his turn in the same car prior to the start of Sunday's grand prix.

Ferrari has detailed that the car will be operated by its F1 Clienti department and will use an “advanced sustainable fuel developed specifically by Shell, drawing on the know-how acquired this season to create the fuel being used in 2026.”

Three of Schumacher's Ferrari cars will also be on display throughout the weekend at Monza.

They will be the 1996 F310 and the 2006 248 F1, Schumacher's first and last cars with Ferrari, as well as the F2002.

title: Jenson Button details Fernando Alonso hope ahead of ‘difficult’ future decision
excerpt:
2009 F1 champion Jenson Button has detailed that he hopes Fernando Alonso will continue to compete in the sport next year.

The two-time champion has not yet declared whether he will carry on his F1 career with Aston Martin amid its disappointing campaign thus far.

The 2026 challenger from the Silverstone-based squad has been languishing well down the pecking order, with a Honda power unit that has also lacked performance.

Alonso insisted he would use the summer break to reach a decision, but so far is yet to declare his intentions for 2027.

Button, however, who is a former team-mate of Alonso, thinks the 45-year-old still has plenty to offer.

“I retired aged 36, nine years younger than Fernando, but I was ready,” Button said.

“I’d spent a couple of years struggling with racing because I didn’t really want to be there. It felt like there wasn’t anything new for me to achieve and when you get to that point you know it’s time to go.

“But I think the difference for Fernando is there’s still an exciting challenge in front of him.

“Obviously, this year has been tough, but it’s still an exciting time to be at Aston Martin Aramco and to be working with people like Adrian Newey. Any F1 driver would love to race a car designed by him, and to experience firsthand him driving this team forward.”

Alonso has been in this situation before, having opted to walk away from F1 at the end of 2018 to pursue different projects.

However, his next decision to exit the sport will likely be with the understanding that there will be no return again in the future.

“I know how difficult it is to decide your future, and he’s been there once before,” Button added.

“He left the sport and came back, so he obviously left too early. Now, he will make sure that he’s 100 per cent certain that he doesn’t want to be in the sport before he leaves.

“Fernando’s still got so much more to give in F1. I would love to see him in an Aston Martin fighting for wins. That’s where he should be, and it’s where this team is aiming to be. He hasn’t won as much as he should have.

“He’s found himself in unlucky situations a few times, one alongside me, but the talent and hunger is still there, which is the key to staying in the sport and being competitive.”
